sections.title: The After-Blessing
sections.html:
Just as the Sages instituted that a person recite a blessing before he eats, so they instituted that he recite a blessing after he eats. However, there is a difference between the first blessing and the after-blessing. The first blessing is meant to thank God for the enjoyment a person has from the food, and the Sages said (Berakhot 35a) that since it is a clear logical principle that it is forbidden for a person to enjoy anything in the world of the Holy One, blessed be He, without a blessing, there was no need for the Torah to command us about it.

But after eating, from logic alone we would not have known that one must recite a blessing, because after we have thanked God with the blessing before eating, seemingly there is no further need to bless again after eating. Therefore the Torah needed to command us specifically that after we have eaten and are satisfied, we should bless God with a comprehensive blessing, not only for the food we ate but for all the good that God has given Israel, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." As we learned at length regarding Birkat Ha-mazon (4:1-4), after a person has eaten and is satisfied, he is liable to become arrogant and to be swept after desire and materialism. On the other hand, through the good taste of the foods and through the vitality he draws from them, he can rise to a broad view of all the good that God has given Israel. Therefore in Birkat Ha-mazon we do not thank God for the food alone; rather, from it we rise to a comprehensive blessing and thanksgiving for the good land and for everything connected with it – the covenant, the Torah, Jerusalem, the kingship of David and the Holy Temple. Through this, the food we ate is also elevated and uplifted, and vitality is added to it for the good. One who does not recite a blessing after eating does not elevate the spiritual side of the food and is not uplifted by it, and consequently the food in his innards becomes coarse and pulls him downward (see above 1:5).

As an extension of the Torah commandment, the Sages instituted that even one who is not satisfied, if he ate the volume of a kezayit, should recite an after-blessing. Over bread he recites Birkat Ha-mazon; over the seven species for which the Land of Israel was praised he recites Me'ein Shalosh; and over other foods he recites Borei Nefashot.

Why did they institute a blessing over the amount of a kezayit? Because it has a certain importance and benefit. The first blessing is recited over any amount, because it is over the very enjoyment of eating, and whoever enjoys even a little must recite a blessing. But the after-blessing is more comprehensive, and only if some impression of satisfaction from the eating remains can one, from it, contemplate the good that God has bestowed upon the world and recite a blessing. Therefore one who ate less than the measure of a kezayit or drank less than the measure of a revi'it does not recite a blessing (these measures will be explained below, halakhot 5-10).

Since the first blessing is over the enjoyment of eating, it must be attached to the beginning of the eating, and it is forbidden to interrupt between the blessing and the eating (above 3:1). But the after-blessing is not over the enjoyment of eating alone, but over the benefit and satisfaction a person has from what he ate; therefore it can be recited even some time later, as long as one feels some satiety from the eating (below, halakha 12).

sections.title: The Me'ein Shalosh Blessing
sections.html:
Over the seven species one recites the Me'ein Shalosh blessing, which is called 'Me'ein Shalosh' ("an abridgment of three") because it contains the essence of the three blessings of Birkat Ha-mazon. Corresponding to the blessing of "Ha-zan" ("who feeds"), one mentions the food that was eaten. Corresponding to the blessing over the Land, one mentions its praise, that it is "a desirable, good and spacious land". Corresponding to the blessing over Jerusalem, one mentions Jerusalem and the Temple. And since after the destruction the Sages added a fourth blessing – Ha-tov Ve-hametiv – they instituted saying corresponding to it as well: "for You are good and do good to all"; yet its name is still 'Me'ein Shalosh', corresponding to the three blessings that must be said by Torah law (Berakhot 44a; MB 208:50; above 4:1-2). The seven species are: wheat, barley, grapevine, fig, pomegranate, olive and date.

Included under wheat and barley are three more species of the grain family: spelt, oats and rye, which together with wheat and barley are the five species of grain. If one made bread from them, one recites Birkat Ha-mazon over it (as explained above 4:1), and if one made from them a cooked dish or a Mezonot baked good, their blessing is like that of the rest of the seven species – Me'ein Shalosh.

The Rishonim disagree about the status of the Me'ein Shalosh blessing. Some say its mitzva is from the Torah, because two verses before the verse in which the Torah commands us to recite Birkat Ha-mazon, the seven species for which the Land of Israel was praised are mentioned, and the implication is that after eating them too one must bless God. As it is stated (Devarim 8:8-10): "A land of wheat and barley, and vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey; a land where you will eat bread without scarcity, where you will lack nothing; a land whose stones are iron and from whose hills you will mine copper. You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." But since there is a difference between eating bread, which is a person's main food, and eating fruits of the seven species, they instituted after eating bread to thank and praise God in a detailed formulation of three blessings, whereas after eating fruits of the seven species they instituted a single blessing, Me'ein Shalosh (Behag, Rosh and Rashba). Others say that by Torah law one is obligated to recite a blessing only after eating bread, since only bread is mentioned in the verse adjacent to the commandment. As an extension of this, the Sages instituted reciting Me'ein Shalosh after eating the seven species, for since the Land of Israel was praised for them, it is fitting, upon eating them, to say an important blessing (Rambam and Semag).1

The Me'ein Shalosh blessing is special: since it was instituted for the species for which the Land of Israel was praised, the Sages instituted that the kind of food be specified explicitly. Over baked goods or cooked dishes made from species of grain, one says: "for the sustenance and for the nourishment" (al ha-miḥya ve-al ha-kalkala). Over fruits of the seven species, which are olive, date, grape, fig and pomegranate, one says: "for the tree and for the fruit of the tree" (al ha-etz ve-al pri ha-etz). And over wine one says: "for the vine and for the fruit of the vine" (al ha-gefen ve-al pri ha-gefen).

On Shabbat, Yom Tov and Rosh Ḥodesh, one mentions the special day in the blessing, for a person's eating on a weekday is not like his eating on a sanctified day. If he forgot and did not mention it, he has fulfilled his obligation. On Ḥanukka and Purim, which are festivals instituted by the Sages, one does not mention the day (SA 208:12).

Since the foundation of the mitzva to thank God for the food is connected with the praise of the Land of Israel, if the fruit grew in the Land of Israel, one is careful to note this in the concluding formula of the blessing: "for the land and for its fruits" (al ha-aretz ve-al peiroteha). And if the fruit grew outside the Land, one concludes "for the land and for the fruits" (al ha-aretz ve-al ha-peirot). Likewise regarding wine: if its grapes grew in the Land, one concludes "and for the fruit of its vine" (ve-al pri gafnah); outside the Land: "and for the fruit of the vine" (ve-al pri ha-gefen). When there is a doubt whether the fruits and grapes grew in the Land, one says the general formulation used outside the Land (Berakhot 44a; MB 208:54).2

sections.title: Laws of the Me'ein Shalosh Blessing
sections.html:
It is proper to be careful to recite the Me'ein Shalosh blessing in the place where one ate and while seated, for some hold that the laws of the Me'ein Shalosh blessing are like the laws of Birkat Ha-mazon (SA 183:10; 184:3; and see above 4:13-14).

If one ate Mezonot, drank wine and ate fruits of the seven species, he mentions all three in the blessing according to the order of their importance: Mezonot, wine and fruits (SA 208:12). If he forgot to mention one of them, sometimes what he mentioned includes what he forgot and exempts it be-di'avad, and sometimes it does not include it, and he must recite the blessing again.3

If one ate Mezonot in an amount that obligates an after-blessing, and a fruit of the seven species or wine in an amount about which there is a doubt whether he became obligated in an after-blessing – since in any case he must recite Me'ein Shalosh for the Mezonot, it is good that he also mention the fruits and the wine in the blessing in order to get out of the doubt (Taz 208:19).

If one ate Mezonot, and his friend ate Mezonot and fruits of the seven species, if the one who ate Mezonot does not remember the blessing well, he may fulfill his obligation by hearing the blessing from his friend, even though his friend also mentions the fruits, for the mention of the fruits is not considered an interruption for him (Birkei Yosef 213:1).

One who eats a kezayit of a fruit of the seven species and additional tree fruits that are not of the seven species recites Me'ein Shalosh and exempts the other fruits as well, for since he gives thanks for the fruits in the Me'ein Shalosh blessing, he exempts all the tree fruits he ate. But if he ate a fruit of the seven species and a fruit of the ground, he recites Me'ein Shalosh over the tree fruit and Borei Nefashot over the fruit of the ground.4

If one drank wine and other beverages – just as before drinking, the Ha-gafen blessing exempts the other beverages (above 7:4), so after drinking, the Me'ein Shalosh blessing over the wine exempts the other beverages (SA 208:15).

sections.title: Borei Nefashot
sections.html:
One who eats the measure of a kezayit of other foods that are not of the seven species, or drinks a revi'it of other beverages that are not wine, recites Borei Nefashot. Originally the Borei Nefashot blessing was optional, and the great Amora Rav would recite it only after eating important foods such as meat and eggs. Over time the custom was accepted as an obligation to recite Borei Nefashot after all eating or drinking (see Berakhot 44b).

Since the first blessing is over the enjoyment of the eating itself, the Sages instituted a special blessing for each kind of food, so that we thank God for every food in a detailed manner. But the blessing after eating is over the general benefit a person derives from the eating, and therefore they instituted one blessing for several kinds. For example, if he ate rice, a tree fruit, a fruit of the ground and meat, and drank juice, he recites four blessings at the outset – Mezonot over the rice, Ha-etz over the tree fruit, Ha-adama over the fruit of the ground, and Shehakol over the meat and the juice. But after eating them he recites Borei Nefashot over all of them, for this blessing exempts all kinds of foods and beverages except for the seven species (SA 207:1).

In the Borei Nefashot blessing we thank and praise God for having created many living beings (nefashot), and for having created all the foods that are essential to supply their lacks so that they can survive; and He further created additional foods so that they might delight in them and with them sustain the soul of every living being. For the delight in the additional foods also adds vitality to a person and enriches his mind and his emotions.

Borei Nefashot is unlike Shehakol. Shehakol is a general blessing and be-di'avad exempts all foods; therefore one who does not know which blessing to recite over a certain food – Mezonot or Shehakol, for example – may recite Shehakol over it. By contrast, with the after-blessing, one blessing does not exempt another: if he is obligated to recite Me'ein Shalosh, he cannot recite Borei Nefashot in its place, and likewise the reverse (MB 202:55).5

sections.title: The Measure of a Kezayit for the After-Blessing
sections.html:
One who eats even a minute amount, since he enjoyed it, is obligated to recite a blessing over it at the outset. But an after-blessing is recited only by one who ate at least the measure of an olive (kezayit), for the Sages said: "There is no eating less than a kezayit." That is, eating less than a kezayit is so little that no impression of satisfaction remains from it over which one could recite a blessing.

As a result of the exiles, a doubt arose about the volume of an olive. Some say that the olive found among us is smaller than the olive the Sages spoke of, which is a little less than a third of an egg. And some say it is about half an egg. And although it appears from many Rishonim that the olive the Sages spoke of is the olive found among us, since we hold the rule "in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient", it was ruled in halakha that one should not recite an after-blessing over less than the volume of half of an average egg of our day. And although it is reasonable that the volume of the olive has not changed, one can explain that since the Jewish people have been accustomed to regard the measure of a kezayit as the volume of half an egg, nowadays, according to our perception, one who eats less than the measure of half an egg is considered to have eaten an amount that has no significance for reciting a blessing over it. And since the basis for setting the measure of a kezayit as obligating an after-blessing is rabbinic, the custom of the Jewish people has the force of a measure set by the Sages.

One need not be anxious about estimating the volume of half an egg, for when people are given something to estimate, without doubt some will err upward and some will err downward, and nevertheless the Sages entrusted these measures to each and every person. In addition, we have learned that according to most Rishonim the measure of an olive is much smaller than half an egg, and already over that amount it would have been proper to recite a blessing according to the essential enactment of the Sages. Therefore, whenever it seems to a person that he ate the volume of half an egg, it is a mitzva for him to recite a blessing.6

sections.title: Volume, Not Weight
sections.html:
The measures the Sages spoke of are measures of volume, not weight. For it is clear that Jews did not walk around with a scale in their pocket, and therefore the Sages gave their measures according to common things, such as an olive and an egg, which can be estimated by sight. As we have learned, the practical ruling is that the measure of an olive is about half an egg. If the food has large hollows, they are not counted toward the volume, but small holes that are not very noticeable do not change the calculation, and whenever it appears that the volume of the food is about half an egg including the small holes, one recites an after-blessing over it.

There were, however, Sephardic poskim who were accustomed to measure the measures by weight, because it is difficult to estimate volume: sometimes the food is long and sometimes square, and sometimes it has large hollows that are not counted toward the volume. In addition, some hold that the small holes too should be subtracted from the measure of volume, and it is very difficult to estimate their volume; therefore they made use of weight. But they too agree that in principle the measure depends on volume and not on weight. This has been the custom of the Jewish people from time immemorial: to estimate according to volume and to include the small holes in the measure, and only the large hollows, which are not part of the texture of the food, were not included in the measure. And this is the halakha.

For example, in bread, the large hollows that sometimes form in it are not included in the measure, but the small holes that run throughout it are included in the measure of half an egg. The same law applies to rice cakes, popcorn, Bamba, whipped cream and the like: since they have no large hollows inside them, one goes according to the volume before us.

Every person should learn to estimate foods relative to half an egg. We have already learned that one need not worry about error, for the Sages gave every person the authority to estimate the measure himself, even though it is quite possible that he will err somewhat upward or downward.7

sections.title: The Measure of Akhilat Peras
sections.html:
If one ate the measure of a kezayit with long pauses, then if from the beginning of his eating to its end less than the time-measure of 'akhilat peras' (the time it takes to eat a peras) passed, his eating is still considered one act of eating, and he recites an after-blessing after it. But if he ate the measure of a kezayit over a longer time, his eating is not considered one act of eating, and he does not recite an after-blessing over it.

A 'peras' is the amount of bread people were accustomed to eat at one meal. But a doubt arose as to how many minutes it actually takes an average person to eat the 'measure of a peras'. According to those who give a longer time – nine minutes; and according to those who give a shorter time – three minutes. In practice, it is good to finish the measure of a kezayit within four minutes; however, even one who ate the measure of a kezayit (half an egg) over about seven minutes is obligated to recite a blessing. For the measure of 'akhilat peras' was set according to people in general, and since quite a few people eat the measure of a peras in about seven minutes, this measure is considered a measure of eating.8

sections.title: Being Scrupulous Regarding the Measures (Beriya and Kezayit)
sections.html:
Some say that one who eats a whole beriya (an entire natural item), such as a single grape, or a pomegranate seed, a chickpea or a pea, must recite an after-blessing. Even though it does not contain the measure of a kezayit, since it has special importance, being a whole entity, one should recite an after-blessing over it (based on the Yerushalmi). And although it was ruled in halakha that whoever did not eat the measure of a kezayit does not recite a blessing (Rif and Rambam), nevertheless le-khatḥila, in order not to enter into a doubt, it is proper not to eat a beriya without eating an amount that obligates an after-blessing (Rosh; SA 210:1). If he bites off a piece of the beriya and afterward eats the rest, since he did not put the whole beriya in his mouth at once, he is not considered as having eaten a beriya (Ben Ish Ḥai, Matot 5). Likewise, if he does not swallow the pit, as with the pit of a date, an olive or a cherry, he is not considered as having eaten a beriya (MB 210:7, 9).9

Likewise, it is proper for those who are scrupulous to eat either less than the measure of our olive, in which case according to all opinions they will not recite an after-blessing; or the volume of half an egg or more, in which case according to all opinions they will recite an after-blessing. But if they eat from the volume of an olive up to less than the volume of half an egg, according to some poskim they will need to recite a blessing, but in practice they will not recite a blessing, for in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient (above, halakha 5).

All this is for those who wish to be stringent with themselves, but according to the letter of the law there is no obligation in this, and one who wants to eat a doubtful amount may do so, and afterward he should not recite an after-blessing, in accordance with the rule that in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient.

sections.title: The Measure for the After-Blessing over Cake
sections.html:
One who eats cake in the volume of a kezayit (the volume of half an egg) recites Al Ha-miḥya. Although among the ingredients of the cake there are eggs, sugar and oil, so that the flour itself that he ate does not amount to a kezayit, since the other ingredients are subsidiary to the flour and are meant to flavor it, they combine with it to make up the measure of a kezayit. This is on condition that the flour is at least one-eighth of the other ingredients (SA 208:9; MB 43, 48). In practice, in almost all our cakes, including whipped [?] (batter) cakes, there is at least one-eighth flour.

If the amount of flour in the dough is less than one-eighth of all the ingredients, after eating a kezayit of the cake one does not recite Al Ha-miḥya but Borei Nefashot. For since the flour in this cake is so little, it does not draw the other ingredients after it but is drawn after them. But before eating it one must recite Mezonot, because regarding the first blessing no specific measure is required; rather, as long as the flour too is meant to give flavor, it is the main ingredient, and the blessing is determined by it (SA 208:2-3; below 11:4).

In a pashtida (savory pie) and a patty, the other ingredients are not meant only to flavor the flour, as in a cake, but have value of their own. Therefore, only if the flour is the majority of the mixture does one recite Al Ha-miḥya over eating a kezayit of the pashtida. But if the flour is the minority, the other ingredients do not combine with it, and therefore only if he ate an amount of a kezayit (half an egg) of the flour itself within the time of akhilat peras (7 minutes) does he recite Al Ha-miḥya – for example, if he ate the measure of three olives in seven minutes from a pashtida whose flour is one-third of all its ingredients. But if he did not eat such an amount, whenever he ate an amount of a kezayit from the pashtida he recites Borei Nefashot.

A cake or pashtida that has a filling that is not mixed into the flour: since the filling stands on its own, it does not combine with the flour, and only if he ate a kezayit of the dough together with all its ingredients does he recite Al Ha-miḥya. If only together with the filling did he eat the measure of a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot. For example, if he ate strudel whose dough does not amount to a kezayit, but together with the apples inside it there is a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot. And if the dough amounted to a kezayit, he recites Al Ha-miḥya (see below, note 14).10

sections.title: The Measure for the After-Blessing over Drinking
sections.html:
One who drinks a 'revi'it ha-log', which is the volume of an egg and a half, is obligated in an after-blessing. Some say that the law of drinking is like the law of eating, and one who drinks the volume of a kezayit – half an egg – is obligated in an after-blessing (Tosafot). Those who are stringent are accustomed to take their view into account and not to drink an amount of more than half an egg and less than a revi'it. However, in practice there is no obligation to take their view into account, and whoever drank less than a revi'it, about 75 milliliters, should not recite a blessing (SA 210:1. This measure is less than half an ordinary cup. In the note it is explained that the measure is 75 ml and not 86 ml).11

The duration: some say that the law of drinking is like the law of eating, and if one drank a revi'it over the time of akhilat peras (7 minutes), he is obligated to recite an after-blessing (Ra'avad). And some say that the law of drinking differs from the law of eating, for since people are accustomed to drink continuously, if one drank the measure of a revi'it more slowly than is customary for drinking a revi'it, he does not recite an after-blessing (MA, based on the Rambam). Since we hold the rule that in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient, whoever drinks a revi'it beyond the time in which it is customary to drink a revi'it does not recite a blessing. But if he drank continuously, with slight pauses for sipping and breathing, he is obligated to recite an after-blessing.

According to several poskim, one who drinks a beverage that people are accustomed to drink slowly, such as hot coffee or soup, even though he did not drink it continuously, recites an after-blessing after it, because this is the manner of drinking it (Ginat Veradim). Some have practiced this way. However, according to many poskim, one should not distinguish between a hot drink and a cold one, and whoever drank the revi'it in more time than people are accustomed to drink a revi'it does not recite an after-blessing. Le-khatḥila, in order to satisfy all opinions, it is good that he eat or drink an additional food or beverage, so that he can recite Borei Nefashot over it without doubt.12

sections.title: Cheese, Leben and Ice Cream Are Treated as Food
sections.html:
We have learned that there is a significant difference between a food and a beverage: one recites an after-blessing over a food in the measure of a kezayit (half an egg) eaten within the time of akhilat peras (7 minutes), and over a beverage in the measure of a revi'it (75 ml, the volume of an egg and a half) drunk continuously in the customary manner. Two main signs distinguish between a food and a beverage. The first is that a beverage is a liquid, and if it is placed on a plate it will spread out in all directions; when it does not spread out to the sides, it is a food. The second is that a food is chewed with the teeth, or at least worked a little with the tongue, whereas a beverage is drunk.

Therefore leben (a cultured milk product), cheese, jelly, pudding and ice cream, since they are not fit for drinking and are worked a little with the tongue, are treated as food, and one recites an after-blessing over eating the measure of a kezayit (half an egg) within the time of akhilat peras (7 minutes). If the leben is shaken until it becomes liquid, its law will be like that of a beverage. And soup, even if it is thick, as long as it spreads like a liquid, its law is like that of a beverage.

An ice pop made of frozen water with sugar: one who sucks or licks it while it is outside his mouth is treated as one who drinks, and since it is not possible for him to manage to suck a revi'it within the time in which people are accustomed to drink a revi'it, he should not recite an after-blessing after it. But if he bites the ice pop, even if afterward he sucks it inside his mouth, it is treated as food, and if he ate of it the measure of half an egg within about 7 minutes, he recites an after-blessing.13

If one drank the measure of a revi'it from two different kinds of beverages whose blessing is the same, or ate the measure of a kezayit from two different foods whose blessing is the same, they combine together to obligate him in an after-blessing. But if he drank half a measure of a beverage and ate half a measure of a food, he does not recite an after-blessing, for the measures of food and drink do not combine (MB 210:1).14

sections.title: Until When One May Recite the Blessing
sections.html:
One must recite the after-blessing immediately upon finishing eating or drinking, and one should not occupy oneself with anything before the blessing. For it is not proper for a person to engage in his affairs before he thanks God for the food he ate, and furthermore, there is a concern that he may become absorbed in his affairs and forget to recite the blessing. In any case, one should hurry to recite the blessing as long as he is enjoying it and feels more satiated than he was before he ate. Be-di'avad, if he delayed and did not recite the blessing, and it is not clear to him that he now feels more satiated than he was before he began eating, if 72 minutes have not yet passed since he finished his eating or drinking, he may still recite the blessing. After that he should not recite it. And if it is clear to him that he still feels more satiated than he was before he ate, he may recite the blessing even after 72 minutes.15

One who eats a satiating meal, even though he did not eat bread, be-di'avad, even if several hours have passed, as long as he feels a sensation of satiety he is obligated to recite the blessing. From the moment he feels a little hungry and begins to want to eat another meal, he has lost the blessing (see above 4:14, in the explanation of this measure).

sections.title: One Who Tastes and Drinks at Intervals: When Should He Recite the Blessing?
sections.html:
Sometimes a person intends to eat several fruits or several kinds of Mezonot over the next few hours, or to drink several cups, and the question arises: is it proper for him to recite one blessing at the beginning over everything he intends to eat and drink, and at the end an after-blessing over everything he ate and drank; or is it more proper for him to recite, over each act of eating and each cup, a blessing before it and a blessing after it? The rule is that if the acts of eating and drinking are considered one continuum, it is preferable to recite one blessing over everything. And if they are considered separate – for example, he pauses between them for a long time, or he eats them in different places – it is preferable to recite a blessing over each act of eating and drinking separately. Sometimes additional factors affect this, such as the placing of the foods [in front of him] or sitting with friends. Let us explain the halakha:

One who sits in one place and intends to pause between one act of eating and the next, and between one drink and the next, for less than half an hour, should properly combine all the acts of eating or drinking, and recite a first blessing over everything at the beginning, and an after-blessing over everything at the end. And if it is likely that he will pause for more than half an hour, since the pause is relatively long, it is preferable that he recite a first blessing and an after-blessing over each act of eating and each drink. In any case, be-di'avad, as long as he pauses less than 72 minutes between one act of eating and the next and between one drink and the next, he may still recite one blessing before all the acts of eating and drinking and one blessing after them.

If he placed in front of him a plate of fruit, a plate of cakes or a pitcher to drink from, since they are in front of him and he intends to continue eating or drinking from them, everything he eats and drinks from them is considered one continuum. Therefore, even if he sometimes pauses for more than half an hour, it is better that he recite one blessing over everything at the beginning, and one blessing after he finishes his eating or drinking. But if he knows that he will pause for more than 72 minutes, he should recite a first blessing and an after-blessing over each act of eating and each drink.

When a group has gathered at a party and has in front of them various refreshments and drinks, their sitting together, in addition to the refreshments before them, binds everything they eat and drink into one act of eating and drinking. They should recite blessings at the beginning over everything they will eat and drink, and after they finish eating and drinking they should recite an after-blessing. For example, if they had in front of them Mezonot, fruits and juice, they should recite at the beginning Mezonot, Ha-etz and Shehakol, and at the end Al Ha-miḥya and Borei Nefashot. Even if several hours pass between the first eating and the end of the party, as long as they are settled there and from time to time they taste the foods and drink the beverages in front of them, they have not lost the blessing over what they ate and drank at the beginning. Some are scrupulous to make sure that 72 minutes do not pass without their eating or drinking something. In any case, even one who paused for 72 minutes without eating or drinking has not lost the after-blessing, since he has not become hungry or thirsty in the meantime, for had he been hungry or thirsty, he presumably would have eaten and drunk more of what was in front of him.16
